quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Audience, Offer, and Core Persuasion
quizzes.intro: Check foundations before CTAs, ethics, and advanced practice.

questions.prompt: What should come before polishing adjectives in copy?

options.text: A clear sense of audience and offer
As many buzzwords as possible
A fake countdown timer
Removing the call to action

questions.explanation: Audience and offer clarity make persuasion possible; adjectives cannot rescue a muddy offer.

wrongExplanations.c: Fake urgency is an ethics and trust problem, not a foundation.
wrongExplanations.d: CTAs matter later; they are not the first planning step.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a feature and a benefit?

options.text: They are identical terms
A feature is what something has or does; a benefit is why that matters to the reader
A benefit is always a technical specification
Features are unethical by definition

questions.explanation: Strong copy translates features into meaningful outcomes while keeping some features as proof.

wrongExplanations.a: The lesson treats them as distinct and complementary.
wrongExplanations.d: Features are useful when translated and evidenced.

questions.prompt: Which headline approach best matches the lesson?

options.text: Clever wording that hides the offer
A specific promise or audience-problem line that earns the next sentence
Only the company founding year
A wall of synonyms

questions.explanation: Headlines should earn attention from the right reader with clarity and relevance.

wrongExplanations.a: Cleverness without clarity is a listed failure mode.
wrongExplanations.c: Company history rarely belongs in the hero headline.
wrongExplanations.d: Synonym stuffing is not persuasive structure.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the persuasion stack?

options.text: Attention, relevance, value, proof, objections, and action
Only jokes and no ask
Feature dumps with zero outcomes
Hiding pricing forever as a principle

questions.explanation: The stack is a drafting spine from attention through a clear next step.

wrongExplanations.b: Entertainment without action is not conversion copy.
wrongExplanations.d: Transparency about cost is often necessary for trust.

options.text: Because vague superlatives are always legally required
Because concrete claims are more believable and useful to the reader
Because readers dislike examples
Because specifics remove the need for proof

questions.explanation: Specific promises help readers test fit and trust; empty hype does not.

wrongExplanations.a: Superlatives are not a legal requirement of good copy.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — CTAs, Proof, and Ethical Conversion
quizzes.intro: Test calls to action, proof, objections, and ethics.

options.text: Vague labels like “Submit” or “Click here” with no context
A clear action that names the value, matched to commitment level
Five equally loud primary buttons
No CTA so readers guess

questions.explanation: CTAs should instruct and fit how much commitment the reader is ready for.

wrongExplanations.a: Vague buttons hide the next step.
wrongExplanations.d: Conversion copy needs an explicit ask.

options.text: “Great product!” with no detail
A specific result with context, such as cutting onboarding from 9 days to 4
Invented testimonials
Unverifiable “#1 in the universe” claims

questions.explanation: Specific, contextual proof builds belief; vague or fake proof undermines trust.

wrongExplanations.a: Vague praise is weak social proof.

options.text: Using different promises in ads and landing pages on purpose
Keeping the ad promise consistent with what the landing page delivers
Matching font sizes only
Removing all CTAs after the ad click

questions.explanation: Message match reduces bounce from paid or promotional traffic.

wrongExplanations.a: Mismatch creates distrust and wasted spend.
wrongExplanations.c: Visual details matter less than promise consistency here.

options.text: Fake scarcity countdowns with no real limit
Honest limits, clear pricing/cancellation, and truthful outcomes
Shame-based panic as the default strategy
Hiding who testimonials come from when rules require disclosure

questions.explanation: Sustainable conversion respects truth and reader autonomy.

wrongExplanations.c: Predatory emotional pressure is called out as unethical.
wrongExplanations.d: Disclosure and honesty matter for proof.

questions.prompt: How should objections be handled in copy?

options.text: Ignore them until angry support tickets appear
Answer major hesitations near decisions with FAQs, comparisons, and honest boundaries
Mock the reader for hesitating
Claim every product is for everyone

questions.explanation: Objection handling builds trust and reduces friction before the ask.

wrongExplanations.a: Late answers cost conversions and goodwill.
wrongExplanations.d: Clear “not for you if…” can increase fit.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Craft, Editing, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on research, editing, collaboration, and professional standards.

questions.prompt: Where should voice-of-customer language often come from?

options.text: Only internal roadmap jargon
Support tickets, sales calls, reviews, and customer conversations
Random dictionary words
Competitor insults only

questions.explanation: Customer language research outperforms internal jargon for resonance.

wrongExplanations.a: Roadmap language often mismatches buyer words.

questions.prompt: Which editing question is essential for copy?

options.text: Can I add more unverifiable hype?
Is the offer obvious in about ten seconds?
Did I remove the CTA on purpose?
Did I make the audience unrecognizable?

questions.explanation: The ten-second offer test is a practical clarity gate taught in the lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a soft CTA example?

options.text: “Buy now” as the only option for cold traffic always
“Watch a 90-second demo” or “See pricing” when commitment should be lower
No link anywhere
“Submit” with no context

questions.explanation: Soft CTAs match earlier awareness and lower risk tolerance.

wrongExplanations.a: Hard CTAs too early are a common mistake.
wrongExplanations.c: There should still be a next step.

questions.prompt: How should AI assistants be used in copywriting?

options.text: As the final authority on claims and tone with no review
As a brainstorming aid while humans remain accountable for truth and judgment
To invent testimonials automatically
To replace customer research entirely

questions.explanation: AI can draft alternatives; accountability stays with the writer.

wrongExplanations.a: Unreviewed AI output risks false claims.
wrongExplanations.d: Customer language still requires real research.

questions.prompt: What should a pricing page usually clarify?

options.text: Cute plan names with no who-it-is-for guidance
Who each plan is for, key differences, and how billing/trials work
Only a mysterious “Contact us” for every ordinary buyer
No mention of annual versus monthly options when both exist

questions.explanation: Clear plan fit and billing details reduce friction and distrust.

wrongExplanations.c: Gatekeeping ordinary pricing often hurts conversion.

questions.prompt: Which standard captures the course’s end goal?

options.text: Write so a busy stranger can tell what you offer, why it matters for them, and what to do next
Write to maximize cleverness even if the offer is hidden
Write only for the founder’s ego
Write hype that cannot be defended

questions.explanation: Reader-clear offers and actions are the professional standard throughout.

wrongExplanations.b: Cleverness without clarity is a failure mode.
wrongExplanations.c: Founder-centric copy is a listed mistake.
